national.title: Why did California's billionaire tax fail to surf the blue wave?
national.summary: Two economists debate what California's vote on Prop 40 means for the wealth tax movement.
national.body:
Late Monday, The Associated Press determined that California voters had rejected Prop 40, the proposed billionaire wealth tax I wrote about last week . Given the big blue wave we saw during the midterms, why did this tax on billionaires fail to surf to victory?

To make sense of the results, I went back to the two economists I spoke with last week: UC Berkeley's Gabriel Zucman, a leading champion of wealth taxes, and Stanford's Joshua Rauh, a prominent critic of Prop 40.

Last week, they disagreed on what this wealth tax on billionaires would do to California's economy and tax revenue. Now comes the sequel, in which they disagree on what the results say about the politics of wealth taxes.

Their debate could foreshadow a bigger one in the next Democratic presidential primary: should the party embrace a wealth tax?

Zucman blames the corrosive influence of money for Prop 40's failure.

"I am not surprised," Zucman says. Opponents of Prop 40 spent almost $400 million fighting it, including spending on competing ballot measures, making it one of the most expensive ballot initiative fights in history.

"The money spent by the billionaires was critical," Zucman says. "Anyone who lives in California has been carpet-bombed by a deluge of ads. One can easily see how this could be pivotal in such a closely contested ballot."

But didn't Democrats win plenty of races this cycle despite huge sums spent against them? In Texas, for example, Elon Musk alone poured more than $150 million into defeating Democrat James Talarico. And Talarico ended up winning his Senate race by a comfortable margin . Why would money have been so decisive with Prop 40 and not in other races around the nation?

national.title: Police officer dies and another injured after backpack explosion in Oviedo
national.summary: Officers attended the scene in connection with a separate incident at a residential building in the city.
national.body:
A police officer has died and another has been injured in the northern Spanish city of Oviedo after an explosive device went off at the scene of a shooting.

The blast happened when officers from Spain's canine unit and explosives disposal unit arrived and examined a suspicious backpack following reports of a dispute between neighbours on Tuesday morning .

A woman who had been shot and the injured officer have been taken to hospital for treatment.

The suspect fled the scene and is still at large, police said.

Spanish police paid tribute to the dead officer, who has been named as Juan José, in a statement on X and said: "Our hearts are with his family, friends, colleagues and loved ones."

Officers attended the scene early after receiving reports of an argument between neighbours and upon arriving found a woman who had sustained gunshot wounds, police spokesman Pedro Aguado said.

While searching for the suspected attacker, officers found a suspicious backpack with a flashing light and contacted both the bomb disposal unit and canine unit.

"While the package was being moved outside to ensure the safety of the residents, an explosion occurred," Aguado added.

national.title: Israeli forces kill Palestinian boy in West Bank, health ministry says
national.summary: The Israeli military says its soldiers opened fire at individuals “who intended to hurl stones” at a road used by Israelis.
national.body:
Israeli forces have shot dead a 14-year-old Palestinian boy during an operation in the occupied West Bank, Palestinian officials say.

Moataz Daghlas was killed on Monday evening in the village of Burqa, north-west of Nablus, according to the Palestinian health ministry.

The Israeli military said soldiers identified "several terrorists who intended to hurl stones" in an area where stones had previously been thrown at Israeli vehicles. The soldiers fired towards them "to remove the threat", it added.

The Palestinian Red Crescent said its teams treated two people with gunshot wounds, but that Israeli forces blocked their access to a third wounded person and detained three volunteer paramedics.

Moataz Daghlas's relatives said Israeli authorities were withholding his body.

Meanwhile, Palestinian news agency Wafa identified the two Palestinians wounded during the raid as a 17-year-old child, who it said was shot in the abdomen and pelvis, and a 19-year-old man, who was shot in the hand.

According to the UN, at least 98 Palestinians, including 22 children, have been killed by Israeli forces or settlers in the West Bank since the start of the year.

Six Israelis, both security forces and civilians, have been killed by Palestinians in the West Bank over the same period, it says.

national.title: Gas prices slip below $4 a gallon for first time since July
national.summary: Petroleum expert Patrick De Haan predicts prices will continue to sink and reach $3.75 a gallon by Thanksgiving.
national.body: Gasoline prices in the U.S. are below $4 a gallon for the first time in nearly four months.According to AAA, the national average for a gallon of gasoline was $3.9788 on Tuesday, down from $4.56 a gallon earlier this year.Patrick De Haan, a petroleum expert at tracking firm GasBuddy, predicts that fuel prices will continue to ease into the Thanksgiving holidays.Why are prices down?Gas prices have fallen in recent weeks as filling stations switch from summer-blend fuels to cheaper winter blends. Federal rules require gas stations to sell a summer blend, designed to guard against evaporation, from June 1 to Sept. 15. Outside that period, stations are allowed to use a winter blend, which is cheaper to produce, explaining why prices often fade in the fall.The switch to the winter blend coincides with a drop in demand, as people take fewer road trips and vacations during the winter months. According to AAA, gas prices fall by around 10 to 30 cents per gallon during the winter months for that reason.Global oil costs, the main factor determining prices at the pump, have also dipped amid hopes that the midterm elections could open the door to a deal between the U.S. and Iran to end the war.On Tuesday morning, futures for Brent crude, the international benchmark, were trading at $91.12 per barrel.

Mr. Trump's former chief of staff, Susie Wiles, worked at the firm for nearly a decade as a managing partner, leaving in 2019.Means claimed Ballard Partners' rise to become the top-earning lobbying firm "did not happen by accident." national.title: U.S.-mediated talks on ending Russia-Ukraine war begin in Abu Dhabi
national.summary: The two-day session in the UAE's capital, Abu Dhabi, is the first such meeting since February. It will focus on security guarantees, the White House said before the discussions.
national.body:
Crosses bearing the names of Viktor Fomenko, Natalia Karapetian and Andrii Anikin, killed in a Russian airstrike that destroyed an underground school in Komyshuvakha, lie in a cemetery in Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine, Saturday, Nov. 7, 2026. Evgeniy Maloletka/AP hide caption

ABU DHABI, United Arab Emirates — Three-way talks between Russia, Ukraine and the United States opened Tuesday in the United Arab Emirates, as Washington renews its push to end the war that followed Moscow's all-out invasion nearly five years ago.

Ukraine invasion — explained Europe to join U.S.-brokered Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi, defying Kremlin objections The two-day session in the UAE's capital, Abu Dhabi, is the first such meeting since February. It will focus on security guarantees, the White House said before the discussions. Russia sees NATO as a threat, and Ukraine wants to prevent future Russian invasions.

Hopes of progress in ending Europe's biggest conflict since World War II are tempered by the absence of any significant breakthroughs in three previous rounds of talks early this year. The war has already killed hundreds of thousands of soldiers and thousands of civilians, analysts and humanitarian organizations say.

There are no signs the fighting is abating, and the talks took place against a backdrop of new long-range strikes between Russia and Ukraine. The two armies are largely deadlocked on the front line.

Russia launched 162 drones of various types and a ballistic missile at Ukraine overnight, Ukraine's air force said.

Meanwhile, Russia's Ministry of Defense said that its forces shot down 155 Ukrainian drones overnight above eight Russian regions, as well as the Crimean Peninsula, which Russia annexed from Ukraine in 2014.

U.S. President Donald Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, said on X that he and fellow envoy Steve Witkoff were working on a "negotiated solution that can deliver lasting peace and create the conditions for a sovereign, secure, and prosperous Ukraine within a more stable European security environment."

national.body: The U.S. military moved nine Stratotanker refueling planes from a base in England to facilities in Germany and Spain on Monday, and The Wall Street Journal quoted sources as saying they had been repositioned due to a threat from Iran.It is unclear whether the threat was imminent or general, the sources told the newspaper.CBS News Confirmed found public aircraft tracking data showing 10 KC-135 Stratotankers were moved from Royal Air Force Base Mildenhall, in southeast England to other locations. One landed at Glasgow Prestwick Airport in Scotland, while four went to Spangdahlem Air Base in Germany and one landed at Ramstein Air Base, the headquarters of the U.S. Forces Europe, also in Germany. Four more Stratotankers left Mildenhall and arrived Monday at Morón Air Base in southern Spain."We take proactive measures to ensure our aircraft, our people, and our installations remain safe and secure," a U.S. official told CBS News on Tuesday, without commenting on specific aircraft movements. Three U.S. Osprey tiltrotor transport planes also departed RAF Mildenhall and arrived Tuesday at RAF Lakenheath, another base used by the U.S. in England. It is unclear whether all of the movements were linked to the reported threat from Iran.A U.S. Air Force spokesperson told CBS News that aircraft routinely "rotate between installations and operating locations for a variety of reasons including training and real world requirements." The spokesman added that "U.S. military aircraft are hosted in accordance with access, basing, and overflight agreements with our Allies and partners. Due to operations security, we will not provide further information on movement of assets."The U.S. Air Force 100th Air Refueling Wing, which has been based at RAF Mildenhall for years, did not immediately respond to CBS News' request for comment on the aircraft movements. The 100th air wing is the only permanent U.S. refueling wing in Europe. national.summary: "This irredeemable body makes a mockery of human rights through consistent failures to uphold its own 'values' as it pushes anti-American rhetoric," a State Department spokesperson said.
national.body: Geneva — The United States is set on Tuesday to become the first country to fully shun a regular review of its human rights record at the U.N.'s top rights body since it was created two decades ago.The Trump administration last year pulled the U.S. out of the Human Rights Council, accusing it of an anti-U.S. and anti-Israel bias, and alleging that it didn't uphold the very values it promotes. Supporters back the council's mandate to keep tabs on human rights in all U.N. member states including the U.S., which has drawn criticism for its policies including strong-arm deportations and targeted killings of alleged drug-runners in the Caribbean and Pacific — which the administration has said are designed to protect U.S. workers and help keep the country safe. The Geneva-based council regularly examines the rights records of all 193 U.N. member states — generally about every four to five years — as part of a process known as the universal periodic review. The United States, under President Trump, already skipped its appointment for its review a year ago. The scheduled November 2025 review was pushed back until Tuesday in hopes that the U.S. government might change its mind. It did not. "(W)e give no credibility to the agency," a State Department spokesperson said in an email to The Associated Press. "This irredeemable body makes a mockery of human rights through consistent failures to uphold its own 'values' as it pushes anti-American rhetoric," the spokesperson said, alleging the council has a "persistent failure to condemn the most egregious human rights violators." national.title: How word of mouth is helping an Amish community's fight against measles
national.summary: In Pennsylvania, health officials use a quiet vaccination campaign designed to win the trust of the state's Amish community, which has been hit hard by the measles outbreak.
national.body:
Dale Weiser is the clinical services supervisor for the Chester County Health Department. Since August, she's been leading efforts to immunize her county's Amish families against measles in their homes. Weiser poses for a portrait at the Chester County Health Department in West Chester, Pa., on Oct. 28, 2026. Daniel Vasta for NPR hide caption

Measles spreads incredibly fast. For the last few months, so has Dale Weiser's phone number.

Living Better Here's what to know if you're unsure about your measles immunity status Weiser is the clinical services supervisor for the Chester County Health Department in south-central Pennsylvania. Since August, she's been driving out to Amish homes to vaccinate people against measles. She says it usually starts with a phone call.

"I was at a house, like, at 4:30 in the afternoon, and I had a phone call at 8 the next morning saying, 'hey, I heard you were down the street. Can you come do that at my house?'" she says of a typical request she gets from Amish families. So far, she's administered more than 400 doses of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine in Amish homes.

Surveys suggest only about a third of Amish families in the region vaccinate their children. That's left the Amish community especially vulnerable to measles, one of the most contagious diseases.

There's no religious edict against vaccination among the Amish. It's very much seen as a family and individual choice, says Weiser. Often, she says, these decisions are driven by practical and cultural factors.

Animals graze at a farm in Bird-in-Hand, an agricultural community in Lancaster County, Pa., with a large Amish and Mennonite population, on Oct. 29, 2026. Daniel Vasta for NPR hide caption

"They don't have health insurance. They're not interacting with the mainstream medical society. And measles wasn't a problem for 30 years, so there was no real risk to not being vaccinated, at least for measles," Weiser says.

national.title: The Democratic Party gained power across the country in the midterms. Now what?
national.summary: Voters handed Democrats the keys to power across the country and expect them to drive in a different direction. Party leaders are now trying to figure out which way to go.
national.body:
Two years ago, voters sent Democrats a message when they ousted them from power in Washington. At first glance, last week's midterm results sent a new one.

Democrats will enter the next Congress with one of the largest majorities in a generation, flipping dozens of House districts and at least seven Senate seats in mainly Trump-won communities. The party now controls a majority of governorships, and gained control of several additional state legislative chambers.

"I think one of the big surprises for me on Tuesday night was just how deep and wide our election results were," Democratic National Committee Chairman Ken Martin said in an interview with NPR. "This was the biggest election cycle for Democrats in the history of our party."

Martin, who has faced criticism from some inside the party throughout his term as chairman, said that the stunning Democratic victories across the country were the result of his party's focus on issues like affordability and ending the war in Iran.

He said the midterms were bigger than politics and bigger than party, and acknowledged the results were just as much about serving as a "massive repudiation of Donald Trump and the MAGA Trumpers and the Republican Party." "I think it's an admonition for Democrats, for sure: Now that we're in power, we have to deliver," he said. "But it was a complete message to Republicans. You had the ability to help us and you did nothing."

With an expanded Congressional majority and a lame duck president, one of the frontlines for figuring out if the Democratic party's power will hold will be in the South, Martin said.

"Six of the 10 fastest growing parts of the country right now are below the Mason-Dixon line, and 40% of the U.S. population is going to live in the South after the next Census," he said. "As we go into 2032 and there's a realignment with the reapportionment, states like Minnesota, Michigan, Wisconsin, Pennsylvania, New York, Rhode Island, Illinois and California are all going to lose electoral votes and congressional votes to the South."

Only on NPR The South flexes political power in midterms, sets regional influence in 2028 election Last week's midterms brought the region's power – especially with Black voters – more squarely into focus. Turbocharged Black voter turnout helped elect the country's first Black female governor in Georgia and may elect the first Black U.S. Senator from Mississippi since Reconstruction.

national.summary: Disgraced British television personality and Hollywood actor Russell Brand has been sentenced to prison for raping a woman in 2009 and sexually assaulting three others.
national.body: Disgraced actor Russell Brand was sentenced Monday to 10 and a half years in prison for raping a woman in 2009 and sexually assaulting three others.The disgraced British television personality and Hollywood actor was convicted last week on one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault, but acquitted on two other counts of rape and an attempted indecent assault charge.A jury of eight men and four women in Southwark Crown Court, in South London, found Brand guilty of groping a woman's breasts at a London bar in 2004, sexually assaulting a woman at a London radio station in 2004 and 2005, and raping a woman at his west London home in 2009.The judge, Joel Bennathan, called Brand a "sexual predator" in his sentencing remarks, saying he displayed "staggering arrogance" and believed that "fame meant you could act ⁠how you liked, when you liked."For the rape he was sentenced to nine years, plus 18 months for the sexual assaults. Brand is expected to serve at least seven years in prison, and the rest of his sentence under heavy restrictions, such as wearing a tag.Six women made the allegations against him, spanning from 1999 to 2009.Before the sentencing Monday, victim impact statements from the women involved in Brand's crimes were read out in court, three by the prosecutor and one by one of the women, who was hidden from everyone but the judge by a screen. "I've been in shock and turmoil for years. I was extremely upset and traumatized. I didn't have any respect for myself," the woman reading her statement said, according to CBS News partner network BBC."I was thinking I was damaged goods - scared of giving off signals that could be taken the wrong way."Another statement, read out by the prosecutor, called Brand "a sexual predator who has no remorse … I just hope he is not allowed to hurt any more women."A third statement, from the woman who Brand was convicted of raping in 2009, said she "struggled to sleep and eat" and "cope with my emotions" after the attack. national.title: Kim Kardashian's Skims offers refunds for $148 advent calendar after backlash
national.summary: The contents of the calendar, including hair clips and keychains, have been widely criticised on social media.
national.body:
Kim Kardashian's Skims is offering customers refunds for its $148 (£110) advent calendar which has been widely criticised on social media.

The accessories advent calendar promised "twelve days of fun surprises" but has been mocked online for the quality of its contents, such as hair clips and keychains, with some comparing them to something you would find down the back of a sofa.

A spokesperson for Skims has told a number of media outlets "for some, the calendar didn't meet expectations" and the company has "personally contacted every customer" to offer a full refund or credit to put towards other products".

The shapewear and clothing business was co-founder by Kardashian in 2019 and has made the reality TV star a billionaire, according to Forbes magazine.

Skims was valued at $5bn in 2025 when it raised millions of dollars in new funding.

One account on TikTok called spicychathouse compared the contents of the calendar to things "my cat collects from around my house". Another account said it looked like "a bunch of stuff that Kim Kardashian was emptying out of her bedside table".

A number of accounts showed people cleaning out their own sofas and claiming they had accidentally created the Skims advent calendar.

What is the most money you’ve spent on an advent calendar, and was it worth it? Let us know.

national.title: Trump says more US attacks on Iran 'highly unlikely'
national.summary: The president says the US is keeping "status quo" with Iran but remains “locked and loaded” should the situation change.
national.body:
Donald Trump has said "Iran militarily is effectively over", and said that there is "positive momentum" behind negotiations to end the Middle East conflict.

"We're just keeping it the status quo," the US president said on Monday. "And we're doing that really at the behest of countries that are their neighbours."

Trump's comments came after he met the Qatari prime minister. Qatar is a US ally in the Gulf region, and one of Iran's neighbours, which has been a key mediator in efforts to end the war.

Addressing reporters in the White House press briefing room, Trump said that renewed US attacks on Iran were "highly unlikely" but that the US was "locked and loaded" should the circumstances change.

Iranian officials have repeatedly expressed doubts about Trump's prior comments about resolving the conflict.

This is not the first time that Trump has said the Iran war is "militarily" over, but the circumstances for him are different now.

The president has hinted at de-escalation in Iran after a bruising set of midterm election results for the Republicans last week, which senior figures including Vice-President JD Vance blamed on the Iran war.

Ahead of the midterms, Trump had said US forces conducted what he described as "minor strikes" on an Iranian island in the Strait of Hormuz . However, in an interview with 60 Minutes that aired on Sunday, the president said that he did not currently see "any reason" to escalate the conflict.

national.summary: The Paris prosecutor's office says investigators have determined that a cyberattack on grocery store chains was "carried out to serve a foreign power — in this case, Iran."
national.body: French officials believe Iran was behind nationwide cyberattacks on commercial refrigeration units at hundreds of grocery stores in October, the Paris prosecutor's office said Monday, accusing a cyber unit of Iran's powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps of carrying out the costly hacks. On Tuesday, France's foreign minister said the country "rules nothing out" in its response to what he called "a terrorist organization that has committed an attack of unprecedented scale and aggression against our country." The Oct. 11 hacking attack struck major supermarket chains, hitting "700 retail locations across France," according to the prosecutor's office, which said the attack caused "significant food spoilage and triggered roughly twenty fires" as the temperatures in refrigeration units shot up.The attacks on the French grocery store chains were followed weeks later by similar hacks affecting refrigerators and freezers at supermarkets in Belgium, Luxembourg and Sweden. national.title: Ukraine peace talks resume with 'some flexibility' by warring sides, US officials say
national.summary: Kyiv, Washington and Moscow have all sent delegations to the United Arab Emirates for the first trilateral talks since February.
national.body:
Trilateral talks between Ukraine, Russia and the US aimed at ending the war in Ukraine have begun in Abu Dhabi.

Although expectations for a breakthrough that ends Russia's full-scale war on Ukraine are low, US officials said yesterday that Moscow and Kyiv were privately showing "a little bit of flexibility" on the issue of who would control Ukraine's eastern regions in a postwar scenario.

Jared Kushner - Donald Trump's son-in-law and part of the US delegation alongside peace envoy Steve Witkoff - said the talks would be focused on addressing the "postwar security concerns" of both Russia and Ukraine.

"An important part of this process is encouraging all parties to begin thinking seriously about what comes after the war," Kushner wrote on X.

Ahead of the meeting, the two US envoys met Ukrainian and European and Nato officials in Abu Dhabi, and French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot was adamant that France, the UK and Germany "will indeed be in the meeting room".

European officials are wary of Russia trying to secure a deal with the US on future "collective security" without them, and Moscow and Kyiv's positions on ending the conflict are still far apart.

A key area of disagreement between the two involves Ukraine's eastern region of Donetsk, which is by now mostly occupied by Russia.

Moscow has demanded that Ukraine relinquish the parts of Donetsk which it still holds, while Kyiv wants to freeze the contact line to maintain control over those sections, which it says are crucial to its future security.

national.title: U.S., Russia and Ukraine start talks aimed at ending war
national.summary: It is the first such trilateral diplomatic push since negotiations were suspended following the start of the war with Iran.
national.body: The United States, Ukraine and Russia have started talks in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday aimed at ending the war in Ukraine that began in 2022 when Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of his country's neighbor.The two-day session is the first such meeting since February and will focus on security guarantees, a long-running demand from Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.President Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner said in a post on X that he and Special Envoy Steve Witkoff were "working hard to find a negotiated solution that can deliver lasting peace and create the conditions for a sovereign, secure, and prosperous Ukraine within a more stable European security environment."Kushner indicated these talks are just an initial step but could "build momentum" toward future negotiations. He also suggested a future agreement would involve a security arrangement involving European countries and Russia.Putin has previously said he wanted Ukraine to pull its troops back from Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson, the four regions Moscow illegally annexed in September 2022 but never fully captured. He also demanded that Ukraine abandon its bid to join NATO, accept strict limits on its military and drop restrictions on the Russian language and the Moscow-affiliated Orthodox Church in Ukraine.Zelenskyy rejected Putin's demands to voluntarily cede territory that Russia hasn't been able to take on the battlefield. Zelenskyy also rejected any limits on Ukraine's military or its arrangements with Western partners, which Kyiv sees as essential security guarantees to stop Moscow from invading again.Ukraine argues that an immediate ceasefire is the necessary first step toward negotiating a wider settlement and says a direct meeting between Putin and Zelenskyy is the only way territorial issues can be settled.The U.S., Russia and Ukraine have held three other rounds of trilateral talks this year, in January and February, but diplomatic efforts largely stalled after Mr. Trump launched a war on Iran. Since then, Witkoff and Kushner have held various separate meetings with Putin and Zelenskyy.In October, first lady Melania Trump's office said she had secured a temporary ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine for the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky for humanitarian reasons. It lasted from Oct. 28 to Nov. 1.

national.title: DR Congo sentences 66 soldiers to death for being 'cowards'
national.summary: The Congolese army's fight against rebel groups has long been hampered by disarray within its ranks.
national.body:
At least 66 soldiers have been sentenced to death in the Democratic Republic of Congo for cowardice, mutiny and refusing to obey orders, local media report.

The sentences followed a trial of 71 soldiers before a military court in Walikale, in North Kivu province, in eastern DR Congo. Four soldiers were acquitted, while another was sentenced to 10 years in prison.

The army said the trial was intended to improve discipline among troops as they battle armed groups in eastern DR Congo.

The region has endured decades of conflict, with fighting continuing between government forces and the Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN), a rebel coalition that includes the M23 group.

The soldiers were reportedly arrested on 20 October in Walikale, where they were accused of abandoning their positions and fleeing during clashes with FRN fighters.

The Congolese army's campaign against armed groups, including the M23, has long been undermined by poor discipline and disorganisation within its ranks.

The government has repeatedly accused neighbouring Rwanda of supporting the M23, an allegation denied by both Kigali and the rebels despite overwhelming evidence.

The army has faced persistent criticism over its lack of professionalism and disciplined, while soldiers have complained of poor pay and inadequate equipment.

national.title: Trump says FBI investigating Nvidia boss's affair with alleged Chinese spy
national.summary: The US president said he spoke with Jensen Huang on Monday and asked him about the affair with the alleged spy.
national.body:
US President Donald Trump has said the FBI is investigating the affair between the chief executive of Nvidia and an alleged Chinese spy.

Trump said he spoke to Jensen Huang on Monday following reports that the US believed he had been targeted in a Chinese espionage campaign.

"I asked him that question, 'Did you have any idea she was a spy?' He said 'I had no idea she was a spy' and I really believe him," Trump told reporters.

Beijing has rejected claims that Huang was targeted, with its foreign ministry saying the allegations were "entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China".

Speaking later at a White House press briefing, Trump told reporters, "I know the FBI is looking into" the affair but did not give further details on the investigation, or confirm when it was launched.

Trump added he thought that Huang was an "honourable guy and I feel very confident that he will be in good shape" after the investigations.

Nvidia, which has commissioned an independent investigation into the affair involving Alice Huang, alleged to be a Chinese spy, said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised.

Nvidia is the world's second most valuable company after Apple, and designs computer chips that have become central to AI technology.

national.title: Oxford museum returns ancestral Naga skulls to India
national.summary: The remains will be taken to Nagaland, where tribal leaders plan a joint memorial and burial.
national.body:
The University of Oxford has returned the remains of 39 people taken from the Naga community during British colonial rule in India.

A delegation of around 30 people from Nagaland, a mountainous state in north-eastern India, attended a ceremony at Oxford's Pitt Rivers Museum on Monday to mark the handover.

The remains, most of which are skulls, will be taken back to India and given what Naga tribal leaders have described as a "respectful rest". There are plans to bury them under a joint memorial in a park in Nagaland.

Museum director Laura Van Broekhoven described it as "a historic moment that will be part of stories told to next generations".

She said the remains were finally on their way home after overcoming "so much red tape everywhere".

The human remains were displayed at the Oxford museum for decades before being removed from public view in 2020 as part of what it described as a "decolonisation process".

The Pitt Rivers Museum holds more than 6,000 objects associated with Naga culture, believed to be the largest such collection in the world. Most were acquired during British colonial rule in India and Myanmar (the former Burma).

These were added to the museum's collection between 1910 and 1940 and mostly collected by two colonial administrators who were anthropologists.

national.title: Polish unity on show as thousands join silent march for Krakow shooting victims
national.summary: Fiercely proud of its reputation for safety, Poland has been profoundly shaken by Saturday's attack, writes Sarah Rainsford.
national.body:
Thousands of people joined a silent march through central Krakow on Monday night, in memory of those killed and injured when a gunman went on a violent rampage at the weekend.

The crowd were led by Poland's president and prime minister, the bitter political rivals putting on a rare show of unity after the country's deadliest attack in modern times.

As they reached the historic Market Square, a bugler played from the tower.

Many people were carrying flowers or candles to leave at the shrines that now dot the cobblestones, each one marking a spot where someone died.

Fiercely proud of its reputation for safety, Poland has been profoundly shaken by this attack. It has left people struggling to make some kind of sense of what happened.

The alleged gunman has been named as 24-year-old Michal Oksinski by local media.

Critically injured in a shoot-out with police, he did not regain consciousness and died in hospital early on Monday .

Initially, the interior minister claimed that Oksinski was driven by far-right, extremist views. The national prosecutor's office now says that it is too soon to say he was "inspired" by any ideology.

national.title: Australia considers criminal penalties for rogue AI in wake of OpenAI hack
national.summary: AI safety regulator will also be created after a rogue OpenAI agent hacked government websites.
national.body:
Australia plans to create a new AI safety regulator and has flagged criminal penalties for tech companies who do not comply, months after an OpenAI hack.

In September, Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese revealed that a rogue OpenAI agent had "infiltrated" a government health website and other systems, and criticised the company for taking months to tell them about the hack.

On Tuesday, he released the 18 recommendations made after a "rapid review" into the breaches including new safety and security standards for AI companies such as mandatory reporting of hacks.

AI brings opportunities, he said, but Australia must prepare for the "new risks" from this "rapidly advancing technology".

"The law needs to get ahead of and, in some cases, make sure that it catches up with, what is a very fast changing world," Albanese said.

One of the recommendations suggests changes to criminal law to have a standalone "failure to prevent" offence .

This would criminalise instances where a company develops "an AI model that engages in harmful conduct" and "fails to take reasonable steps to prevent that harm".

The review also recommended "mandatory, time-bound AI safety reporting" of hacks.

national.title: Californians reject wealth tax for billionaires
national.summary: Proposition 40 targeted Californian billionaires with a 5% tax on their total wealth, including assets such as shares as well as income.
national.body:
California voters have voted to reject a wealth tax on its billionaires.

The ballot proposal would have levied a one-time tax on the state's mega wealthy to help fund healthcare. It took nearly a week of counting votes after the midterm election to determine a projection on the measure.

There are about 200 billionaires in the state, including Meta's Mark Zuckerberg , reality television star Kim Kardashian and media mogul Oprah Winfrey.

Proposition 40 targeted Californians with a wealth of more than $1.1bn (£800m) with a 5% tax on their total wealth, including assets such as shares as well as income. It failed amid divisions among Democrats and labour unions.

Are California voters about to impose 'world's first' tax on billionaires?

Published 24 October Had it passed, experts believe it would have been the world's first wealth tax targeting billionaires.

The tax would have raised about $100bn to make up for federal funding cuts to healthcare in California as a result of President Donald Trump's sweeping tax and spending bill.

Those who backed the measure had argued it would help ensure that the ultra-wealthy were contributing their fair share and helping backfill gaps in the state's budget.

national.title: California voters reject billionaire wealth tax, CBS News projects
national.summary: Voters in California have rejected a tax on the state's wealthiest residents, CBS News projects, following a campaign that has split traditional allies and shattered spending records for a tax-related measure in California.
national.body: Voters in California have rejected a tax on the state's wealthiest residents, CBS News projects, following a campaign that has split traditional allies and shattered spending records for a tax-related measure in California.Proposition 40 would have levied a one-time 5% tax on California residents with a net worth of $1 billion, excluding real estate and certain retirement assets. Proponents of the measure said it was expected to generate $100 billion over five years, with 90% going toward healthcare programs and the other 10% for education, food assistance, and administration of the tax. The proposal came at a time when other states and federal policymakers are debating how to tax extreme wealth and finance public services, and how Proposition 40 was viewed as a bellwether. The vote was framed by supporters as part of a broader struggle over economic inequality and the political influence of the billionaire class. Supporters say the state needs additional money to help offset federal healthcare cuts implemented in 2025 under H.R. 1, known as the "One Big Beautiful Bill Act," and to protect hospitals, emergency rooms, clinics and Medi-Cal services. Proponents also argue that billionaires can accumulate substantial wealth from the stock market and business valuations without paying income tax on those gains until they are realized. They also contend that those who have benefited the most from the state's robust economy should contribute more toward public services.The measure created a divide among politicians and organizations that ordinarily align with Democratic priorities. While it was supported by the California Democratic Party and labor unions including SEIU Healthcare Workers West, the principal sponsor of the measure, it was opposed by Gov. Gavin Newsom, former Orange County Rep. Katie Porter, and major healthcare and professional organizations such as the California Medical Association and California Teachers Association.Newsom and Porter, who have both supported higher taxes on corporations and wealthy individuals, agree with the argument that the proposal would encourage wealthy residents to leave the state and damage its long-term fiscal position by decreasing its tax revenue. national.title: California voters defeat billionaire tax proposal that divided Democrats
national.summary: The novel proposal would have charged billionaires a one-time 5% tax on most of their overall wealth, including their ownership in companies.
national.body:
California voters rejected Proposition 40, the billionaire tax, which had divided Democrats with opponents saying it would drive the wealthy from the state. Jae C. Hong/AP hide caption

California voters have rejected a proposal to charge billionaires a one-time 5% tax on most of their wealth, according to a race call by The Associated Press.

Proponents said the tax could raise $100 billion for healthcare. Led by a union that represents healthcare workers, the SEIU-UHW, advocates of the tax said the Republican-controlled Congress cut healthcare programs to give tax breaks to the wealthy, so it was time for the wealthy in California to fill the gap. The state has more than 200 billionaires, according to estimates, with some putting the number at a few hundred .

Opponents argued that the proposal, known as Prop 40, would just drive the wealthy out of California, costing the state revenue and harming its economy.

But the measure divided Democrats in a state where they heavily outnumber Republicans.

The state's Democratic Party favored Prop 40, as did Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., and Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., who went to the state to campaign for it. But Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom opposed the tax , saying it would be better to have a national tax on the wealthy. The Democratic candidate for governor, Xavier Becerra, also opposed it.

A leading teachers union also opposed the proposal, which would have set aside just a small portion of the resulting revenue for schools. And Google co-founder Sergey Brin led other wealthy Californians in a surge of campaign spending opposing the measure. At least five times as much was spent opposing the measure as favoring it.

Brin also drove a campaign that put two other proposals on the ballot to block the billionaire tax from taking effect, had it been approved by voters.

national.title: These House and Senate midterm races don't have winners yet
national.summary: Democrats won sizable House and Senate majorities in the 2026 midterm elections, but the exact margins are unclear because some races haven't been projected yet. Here's where the results stand.
national.body: Washington — The makeup of Congress shifted dramatically in the 2026 midterm elections, as Democrats decisively won control of the Senate and picked up dozens of House seats — in what's on track to be one of the largest midterm routs in recent decades.The exact margins of Congress are not yet clear, as winners have not yet been projected in two Senate races and more than two dozen House races. They include GOP-held districts with razor-thin margins, a few Democratic seats that could flip to Republicans and several races in California and other Western states that still need to count ballots.Here's a look at the congressional races that CBS News has not yet projected, including where the results stand:Senate Toss-UpsDemocrats are set to enter next year with at least 54 Senate seats, compared to Republicans' 44. Two Senate races still haven't been called — one has long been viewed as a battleground, and the other came out of nowhere.Alaska Senate: Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan is running for reelection against Democrat Mary Peltola, a razor-thin race rocked by a last-minute scandal over how another Dan Sullivan got on the ballot. The count could drag on due to both outstanding ballots and Alaska's ranked choice voting system, which allows voters to rank candidates in order of preference. If no candidate is the top choice of a majority of voters, the last-place candidate is eliminated and the counting process moves to a second round. Final results aren't expected until 15 days after Election Day. Both the Sullivan and Peltola campaigns have argued they have the upper hand.Mississippi Senate: The race between GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith and Democrat Scott Colom was not widely expected to be competitive, but it remains a toss-up. State officials say thousands of mail ballots are outstanding and can legally arrive within five days of the election, and there are an unknown number of "affidavit" ballots from voters whose eligibility needs to be checked. Colom and Hyde-Smith have both predicted that they'll emerge victorious.Democrats on DefenseThe dozens of red districts that Democrats flipped were the primary story of Tuesday night, but a few Republican House candidates are still trying to swim against the tide, either due to redistricting or a favorable local political makeup.Maine's 2nd District: This red, pro-Trump district is one of Republicans' top opportunities

Qantas will outsource 850 local corporate jobs to consulting giant Accenture with most roles moving to India as the airline fast-tracks AI investment.

In an internal email to staff on Tuesday, the Australian company's CEO Vanessa Hudson said "this is hard news for some and I'm sorry for the uncertainty it brings".

The job cuts will begin mid-2027, she said, and start with finance, procurement, people and marketing roles shifting "mostly" to teams in India and "some in Australia" as the firm seeks to modernise its IT systems.

Hudson said the "scale and speed of change in technology and AI is something none of us has seen in our lifetime", and it was in talks with unions and staff on the plans.

The move comes days after the airline provided a market update, flagging fare increases and flight cuts amid higher fuel costs.

On its new multi-year deal with Accenture, Hudson said it was about "modernising" the airline's IT systems to become "more efficient".

Qantas spends more than AU$1bn (US$691m; £514m) a year on technology, she said, and the company's back-end systems needed to be upgraded.

"Like every airline, we run on technology built up over decades for a different era, including more than 1,000 legacy applications that were never designed to work together," she said.

national.title: 'Cruise for life' ship seized in Singapore
national.summary: The Odyssey was meant to take guests around the world for years, but the trip was cut short after its operator ran out of money.
national.body:
A round-the-world cruise that left passengers stranded in Cambodia after its US-based operator ran out of money has been seized in Singapore.

The Odyssey, which set off from Belfast in October 2024 and was meant to take guests on a years-long voyage around the world, is now anchored in Singapore port waters, local authorities say.

Around 200 guests were forced to leave the ship last month in the Cambodian port city of Sihanoukville, after its owner Villa Vie Residences abruptly suspended operations citing "extraordinary increases in fuel costs".

The crew onboard are reported to be well, Singapore's port authority said.

"Arrangements for their welfare and wellbeing are being managed by the vessel's creditors," the authority said, adding that the vessel had been "placed under arrest pursuant to a court order".

Singapore law firm Helmsman LLC has been named the "arresting solicitor", but it is not clear which party it represents.

The Odyssey was meant to go on a three-and-a-half-years voyage covering 150 countries.

Passengers were given the options of buying their cabin outright, which allows them to stay onboard beyond its initial voyage, paying for a five-year residency, or renting a cabin for days-long tours.

national.title: Republican congressman to force impeachment vote on Defence Secretary Hegseth
national.summary: The effort will likely fail, but Representative Thomas Massie wants to push Trump to fire Hegseth before Democrats can launch their own impeachment process next year.
national.body:
A Republican congressman plans to force a vote in the House of Representatives this week to impeach Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, alleging he has violated the US Constitution.

"By engaging in hostilities in Iran for more than 90 days without congressional authorisation, Secretary Hegseth is breaking the law and must be held accountable," Representative Thomas Massie said.

The effort will likely fail, as Republicans remain in power in Congress until January. But Massie says the effort is aimed at pushing President Donald Trump to replace Hegseth before Democrats can launch their own impeachment process.

Hegseth has called the impeachment effort a "sham" and defended his record.

"You see, they attack me. They attack us because we are effective," he said in a video statement last week. "It's not going to work. We will not back down."

He called Massie a "disgruntled, defeated congressman" and said he was not concerned about the impeachment effort. In the video, Hegseth defended his leadership of the department and listed ways he has fulfilled Trump's America First agenda.

Massie formally introduced his articles of impeachment in a resolution on the House floor on Monday afternoon. The move starts a 48-hour clock for the chamber to take up the measure. Lawmakers could vote on the resolution directly, vote to refer it to committee or to set it aside.

"I'm doing this because it's the right thing to do," he told reporters after introducing the articles.

national.title: FDA warns of rare vision-loss side effect from GLP-1 drugs
national.summary: The Food and Drug Administration is adding a new warning about possible rare cases of vision loss reported with GLP-1 drugs like Ozempic, Wegovy and other brands.
national.body: Popular weight loss and diabetes drugs, including Ozempic and Wegovy, will carry a new warning about a possible rare side effect that can sometimes lead to permanent vision loss, U.S. health regulators announced Monday.The Food and Drug Administration said the risk will be added to the labeling of all GLP-1 drugs, the blockbuster medications used to treat obesity, diabetes and several other medical conditions. The class includes a dozen injectable or pill-based drugs, including widely used brands like Zepbound and Mounjaro.The eye condition, known as non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, or NAION, can cause significant vision loss. The problem, which has been reported with all GLP-1 drugs, is caused by decreased blood flow to the optic nerve, although the underlying cause isn't understood, the FDA said.FDA scientists began looking into the problem after the publication of a 2024 medical paper tying the condition to certain patients taking semaglutide, the active drug in Novo Nordisk's Ozempic and Wegovy.Dr. Joseph Rizzo, a neuro-ophthalmologist who co-authored that paper, told CBS News on Monday that he and his team had been working with the FDA to gather and review data on the issue for some time and that, while he didn't know the agency was ready to make a decision, he wasn't surprised it chose to add the warning. He stressed that while he believes the evidence shows GLP-1 usage increases the risk of developing NAION, he doesn't discourage patients from taking them, saying, "The medicines have really been profoundly beneficial to a large number of people."People who aren't on GLP-1s can also develop NAION, which affects somewhere between 2 to 10 of every 100,000 adults over age 50, according to the American Academy of Ophthalmology.Novo Nordisk, the maker of Wegovy and Ozempic, said it "continues to believe the data do not establish a cause-and-effect relationship and we remain confident in the benefit-risk profile of our GLP-1 medicines.""We recognize that NAION can have a profound impact on patients and their families," it said. "Patient safety is a top priority for Novo, and we continue to monitor the safety of our medicines, review new research and work with health authorities around the world."Eli Lilly, which makes Zepbound and Mounjaro, said in a statement Monday it was "carefully evaluating the update and will respond to FDA promptly.""

national.body: A fraternity at Ohio State University has been temporarily suspended while authorities investigate a video that appears to show two panicked men engulfed in flames.A video shared on social media shows a large group of people standing outside, many wearing the school's red and white colors, laughing and shouting while a man sits on the ground with his sweatpants on fire. A woman raped by Jeffrey Epstein says the president of the model agency representing her put her in danger, when he sent her to two photoshoots at the convicted sex offender's Florida beach house.

At the time, in 2009, Epstein was serving a jail sentence for sex offences against a minor but was allowed to work each day from his home.

"My agency's job was to protect me, and they failed. In fact, they put me in danger. And for that, they should be held accountable," she tells the BBC World Service.

Roza was 18 when she was first sent to Epstein's Palm Beach home by MC2 Model Management's US branch, having only arrived in the US from Uzbekistan about a month earlier. MC2's US president at the time, Jeff Fuller, now runs another US model agency called The Source Models.

"My agency knew exactly where I was. So Jeff knew exactly where I was going," says Roza.

She shows us an expense statement suggesting Fuller himself booked her flight home from Palm Beach, following her second shoot at Epstein's home. Fuller has previously claimed he did not know Roza was going to Epstein's house.

She says the photoshoots led to her being employed as an assistant to Epstein. Other survivors have explained how the financier used the recruitment of assistants as an elaborate ruse to allow him to continue abusing young women .

national.title: The superpower battle over energy – and what it means for your bills
national.summary: A tug-of-war between China and the US could have a big impact on energy costs, but who will win?
national.body:
Climate Editor A gas rig in the North Sea. An oil field in Texas. A solar panel factory in China. They can feel a world away, but your energy bill says otherwise.

In January, it could jump by more than a quarter – around £460 extra a year for the typical UK household – according to the latest forecasts from the big suppliers British Gas, EDF and E.ON.

For the second time in four years, a war thousands of miles away is landing in British inboxes.

Since US and Israeli strikes on Iran in February effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, oil and gas prices have soared.

Winter is expected to push them higher still: demand for gas is rising just as Europe's winter gas stores are at their lowest since records began in 2011.

And there's a bigger threat looming over all of this: the warming climate. Cutting carbon emissions is essential to limit future warming and avoid the most damaging effects of climate change. But keeping bills down while cutting emissions is proving hard – and not just for the UK.

As world leaders gather this week in Antalya, Turkey, for COP31, the UN climate summit, the same tension is playing out around the world. Energy and climate policy has become the front line in a contest between the world's two energy superpowers, leaving everyone else squeezed in between.

America is betting on fossil-fuel molecules: pumping record volumes of oil and gas and pressing its allies to buy them. China is betting on electrons: flooding the world with the solar panels, batteries and electric cars that can replace those fuels.

local.title: Pomfret switch boosts city water
local.summary: Dunkirk is thirsty for more revenue, and a significant switchover of Pomfret town water customers will moisten its parched lips. Homes and businesses in Pomfret east and south of the Routes 20 and 60 roundabout were switched over to the North County Water District, and taken off Fredonia’s water sys
local.body:
Dunkirk is thirsty for more revenue, and a significant switchover of Pomfret town water customers will moisten its parched lips.

Homes and businesses in Pomfret east and south of the Routes 20 and 60 roundabout were switched over to the North County Water District, and taken off Fredonia's water system, Friday. The city of Dunkirk water plant on Lake Shore Drive is the NCWD's sole supplier.

City Department of Public Works Director Randy Woodbury mentioned the change at a Monday meeting of the Common Council Finance Committee.

"That will be extra income for the city of Dunkirk," he said.

Officials originally intended to do the switchover Jan. 1, Woodbury said. However, Chautauqua County Health Department officials evidently pushed for an early switch amid the Fredonia water treatment plant's recent problems. The village had boil and conservation orders on water in recent weeks.

Woodbury said the county wanted to lessen the production load for the Fredonia plant. The actual process of the switchover took about 15 minutes, he said. "We're making plenty of water to do it," he added.

The area switched over is growing, and "it's quite a chunk of real estate now on Dunkirk water," Woodbury said.

Councilwoman Natalie Luczkowiak asked if the added revenue was in the city's proposed 2027 budget. Woodbury pointed out that was unlikely as no one knew the move would be made early until Friday.

local.title: Bills pull away from Vikings on MNF 23-6
local.summary: MINNEAPOLIS — Josh Allen threw a touchdown pass with 44 seconds left before halftime, James Cook rushed 31 times for 107 yards and a late score, and the Buffalo Bills beat Minnesota 23-6 on Monday night, sending Vikings deeper into their unrelenting offensive slump. Linebackers Terrel Bernard and Do
local.body:
MINNEAPOLIS -- Josh Allen threw a touchdown pass with 44 seconds left before halftime, James Cook rushed 31 times for 107 yards and a late score, and the Buffalo Bills beat Minnesota 23-6 on Monday night, sending Vikings deeper into their unrelenting offensive slump.

Linebackers Terrel Bernard and Dorian Williams had interceptions and Tyler Bass made four field goals to stretch his franchise-record streak to 25 straight as the Bills (7-1) matched their best eight-game start since 1993. That season ended with their last of four straight Super Bowl losses.

With Kyler Murray sidelined by a hamstring injury, Carson Wentz started at quarterback for the Vikings (6-2) and didn’t finish what became one of the worst performances of his 11-year career. Wentz went 8 for 25 for 81 yards and three turnovers, including a backward pass in the first quarter that was thrown too high for even Justin Jefferson to catch it -- resulting in a lost fumble near midfield.

Wentz, who was checked out in the medical tent at one point for an apparent lower leg injury, was replaced by Max Brosmer midway through the fourth quarter. Wentz completed 1 of 8 passes in the second half.

The battle of Buffalo’s highest-scoring offense in the league against the least-scored-on defense might well have gone to Minnesota had the offense been able to muster a decent drive or two.

But the Vikings had four straight possessions in the first half start beyond their 40-yard line, and the furthest they made it was the Bills 48.

The Vikings as usual sent blitzers at Allen from every angle possible, recording four sacks and an interception of a heave into the end zone that Byron Murphy ran down and returned 55 yards. But the Bills eked out just enough in the first half to give themselves a cushion, when Allen found tight end Keleki Latu open in the back of the end zone for a 25-yard touchdown as he rolled right and was hit hard by Andrew Van Ginkel.

With 322 regular-season touchdowns -- 232 passing, 88 rushing and two receiving -- Allen tied Peyton Manning for the most in NFL history over a player’s first 10 years. Allen is halfway through his ninth season.

local.body:
At its most recent meeting, the Fredonia Board of Education approved probationary appointments for two staff members who were hired as temporary employees pending the fulfillment of necessary requirements. Elizabeth Nau was officially appointed as a Special Education Teacher and Kia Buchanan was officially appointed as a Certified Occupational Therapist Assistant.

Nau was appointed as an Extended Leave Substitute in August as she awaited her teaching certification. Her four-year probationary period of employment as a Special Education Teacher is retroactive to Oct. 6 and runs through Oct. 5, 2030, at which point she can become eligible for tenure.

Buchanan was approved as a temporary hire in early October, beginning her role with the district on Oct. 13. Rather than being appointed for two months as originally approved, Buchanan will now serve in the role of Certified Occupational Therapist Assistant through Oct. 12, 2027.

Additionally, permanent status of employment was granted to Colleen Paradis, Assistant Cook, effective Sept. 9, and to Kiersten Brown, Teacher Aide, effective Oct. 9. Carmen Bonilla resigned from the role of Food Service Helper. Unpaid leave was approved for Kathleen Schutz, Food Service Helper, and Francis Martinez, Teacher Aide.

Chelsi Hilliker was appointed as a full-time Teacher Aide, effective Oct. 23. James Winder's appointment as a full-time Teacher Aide was adjusted, effective Sept. 23. Five substitute teachers were also approved by the Board, including Kayla Sorensen (Certified), Cara Pellechia, Matthew O’Heron, Brittany Morneweg, and Ashley Zielezinski.

Every winter coaching appointment was approved by the Board, including varsity boys basketball coach Nick Bertrando, girls basketball coach Brianne Flowers, boys swimming coach Allie Saye, boys wrestling coach Joe Santilli, girls wrestling coach Ross Conti, boys bowling coach Jim Rush, and girls bowling coach Greg Haase. Board member Jerry Kinney voted against the appointment of Andrew Krenzer as junior varsity girls basketball coach and Tom Stokes as varsity boys indoor track coach, but every other coach was approved unanimously.

The next Fredonia Board of Education meeting will be today at 6 p.m. in the High School Library.

local.title: McGonigle, Stewart are Rookies of the Year
local.summary: Detroit Tigers infielder Kevin McGonigle won the American League Rookie of the Year award and Cincinnati Reds slugger Sal Stewart took home the National League honor Monday night. McGonigle — who played most of the season at just 21 years old — had a .278 batting average and .806 OPS with 18 homers,
local.body:
Detroit Tigers infielder Kevin McGonigle won the American League Rookie of the Year award and Cincinnati Reds slugger Sal Stewart took home the National League honor Monday night.

McGonigle -- who played most of the season at just 21 years old -- had a .278 batting average and .806 OPS with 18 homers, 72 RBIs, 28 doubles and 12 stolen bases while splitting time between third base and shortstop. He’s the first Tigers player to win the award since pitcher Michael Fulmer in 2016 and the first Tigers infielder since Lou Whitaker in 1978.

The Tigers thought enough of McGonigle’s potential that they signed him to a $150 million, eight-year deal in April, just a few weeks into his rookie season. He backed up that confidence with a stellar all-around season that earned him an All-Star nod and helped the Tigers remain in the playoff race for much of the summer.

Stewart was a force in the middle of the Reds’ lineup with 32 homers and 112 RBIs while playing in all 162 games, including 161 starts. He’s the ninth Reds player to win the award and first since infielder Jonathan India in 2021.

McGonigle received 28 of 30 first-place votes and finished with 204 points in balloting by the Baseball Writers’ Association of America conducted before the postseason.

The other two AL finalists were Cleveland Guardians left-hander Parker Messick and Boston Red Sox lefty Payton Tolle. Messick came in second, earning the other two first-place votes and 122 points after going 12-9 with a 2.56 ERA and 193 strikeouts.

Tolle was third with 54 points. He had a 9-6 record with a 3.03 ERA and 171 strikeouts.

Stewart was selected first on 20 of 30 ballots and finished with 170 points.

Taking the highest honor was senior defender Noah Tuah as the Player of the Year leading the defense to the eight clean sheets and a plus-38 goal differential. The Wolverines had three more players join Tuah on the league's First Team with seniors Nolan Anderson and Logan Baum, and junior Braylon Swanson.

Anderson remained one of the top goalkeepers in the league and kept the eight clean sheets along with making 114 saves overall this season. SUNY Fredonia held its annual Veterans Remembrance Ceremony at the Williams Center.

"Thank you to all veterans and active duty service members for your commitment to our defense of the country," SUNY Fredonia President Stephen Kolison said.

Kolison said he has two nephews currently serving in the military. "I can appreciate very much the sacrifice and commitment it takes to stand up and volunteer to be of service to this great nation," he said.

Expressing his "Deep appreciation," Kolison stated "It takes men and women in uniform to protect these rights and privileges we have."

Ava Hartung, a junior music education major native to Fredonia, sang "The Star Spangled Banner." There was a moment of silence for the services and sacrifice of veterans.

Brandon Drummond, a 15-year reservist and a counselor on campus, emceed the event. He explained the World War I origin of Veterans Day, noting that it will always be on Nov. 11 as the original day honored veterans of that war, which ended Nov. 11, 1918.

local.summary: A 7 News investigation found Buffalo Police overtime hours used to meet minimum staffing jumped 65% in a year, with new officers not expected until 2028.
local.body: The Buffalo Police Department doesn't have enough police officers to cover its own contracted minimum staffing levels, forcing a steep rise in the overtime hours needed to keep patrols staffed and 911 calls answered.That's the central finding of my months-long investigation. After filing a Freedom of Information request to the city, I confirmed the BPD is understaffed to the point where it's relying on overtime to meet basic policing needs. And the problem is only going to get worse before it gets better.My FOIL request asked for the number of overtime hours officers are working to cover contracted minimum staffing levels, known as minimum manpower overtime hours.Fiscal Year 2025 to 2026 saw officers undertake 35,526 minimum manpower overtime hours total, a 65% increase on the previous year. That isn't special detail overtime, such as policing Chippewa St. nightlife or the Saint Patrick's Day Parade, but those hours cover the basics such as responding to 911 calls."I'm not going to make light of the situation. We need to hire officers," said Buffalo Police Commissioner Erika Shields. "We inherited this and we are pushing the timeline as aggressively as possible and I sincerely hope we can get officers on board."Some of the minimum manpower overtime hours are covered on a voluntary basis, and sometimes officers are forced to cover the shifts."I don't know that the department needs to be larger than its authorized strength but what I can say is that we definitely need more officers at the rank of police officer," Shields explained.WATCH: 'Crisis mode': Buffalo Police relying on overtime to meet minimum staffing needsThe last time the city administered a police exam for new recruits was in 2023, and Shields says the subsequent three-year pause caused the problem. "There should have been a hiring exam two years ago," Shields said. "And if not two years ago, absolutely last year because there's such a lag time between administering an exam and getting [officers] on the street, you can't wait until you're in a crisis mode."Under previous administrations, the city created and administered its own police exam for $300,000, according to Shields. local.body: Congress is back in session, and Rep. local.title: Rising road maintenance costs put pressure on Town of Colden's proposed 2027 budget
local.summary: Keeping roads safe through a Western New York winter is becoming increasingly expensive, and officials in the Town of Colden say rising costs for road salt, fuel and highway maintenance materials are putting additional pressure on the town's budget.
local.body: Keeping roads safe through a Western New York winter is becoming increasingly expensive, and officials in the Town of Colden say rising costs for road salt, fuel and highway maintenance materials are putting additional pressure on the town's budget.The town is proposing a roughly 24% increase in its highway tax rate as part of its preliminary 2027 budget. The combined amount to be raised by taxation across the town's funds and fire districts would increase approximately 21.6%.Town officials say the highway department accounts for the largest proposed budget increase, driven in part by higher costs for materials and equipment needed to maintain roads throughout the year."Our highway department will be the largest increase and that's due to contracts that are set for the purchase of road salt, trucks to be on the road, as well as our summertime care of the roads," Colden Town Supervisor James DePasquale said.One of the biggest increases is coming from road salt. The town estimates the price will jump from $57.79 to $93.24 per ton, an increase of more than 61%, before an additional fuel surcharge.The town's proposed salt allocation is now expected to reach approximately $127,000.But salt isn't the only expense climbing."There's an increase of almost 40 cents per gallon of road oil and you can use thousands of gallons on a road to maintain it," DePasquale said.WATCH: Rising road maintenance costs put pressure on Town of Colden's proposed 2027 budgetFor a rural community like Colden, keeping roads clear can require significantly more resources than in more densely populated suburbs.Officials say highway crews can make as many as 18 passes on certain roads during a single snow event. During an especially icy stretch, the town could use its entire salt supply in less than a week."We can empty that barn if we have an icy week, we can empty that barn in 5-6 days," DePasquale said.The proposed budget increases the highway department's snow removal allocation from $55,000 in 2026 to nearly $105,000 in 2027.The town says it has already cut more than $120,000 in spending, but continues to face revenue shortfalls and pressure on its available fund balances."We're trying to keep the tax increases as low as possible," DePasquale said.The town's preliminary budget also introduces a $1 tax per $1,000 of assessed value for the general fund, which previously did not have a sepa

local.title: 26 Shirts enters 14th year of giving back
local.summary: 26 Shirts, the Buffalo apparel company founded by Del Reid, is entering its 14th year of turning Buffalo-themed T-shirts into a way to help Western New York families facing serious illness and unexpected hardship.
local.body: What was supposed to be a one-year project has turned into a mission lasting more than a decade.26 Shirts, the Buffalo apparel company founded by Del Reid, is entering its 14th year of turning Buffalo-themed T-shirts into a way to help Western New York families facing serious illness and unexpected hardship.For Reid, it is a career he never expected."Never in a million years would I have thought this was going to be my vocation," Reid said. "I really thought I was just gonna work at a cube for 30 years, retire and then just, you know, be done with my career, but God had other plans."The idea for 26 Shirts developed during the early years of Bills Mafia, as Reid's growing social media presence resulted in families reaching out and asking him to share their stories and fundraisers.Reid says the connection between the two is inseparable."Without Bills Mafia there is no 26 Shirts," Reid said. In 2013, Reid came up with an idea: release 26 Buffalo-themed shirt designs, one every two weeks for one year, with the campaigns helping families in need.The one-year project never stopped.With a typical T-shirt purchase, around $8 goes to the campaign beneficiary."Every family that is approaching us, it's the worst time of their lives," Reid said. "They're going through something that they never, they didn't plan for, they never expected."Reid still remembers how significant the first major fundraising milestone felt."I remember the first time we did a campaign, and we hit $1,000 for a family, and I remember fist pumping," he said. "Yeah, we've raised $1,000 for this family just through stupid T-shirts."That first $1,000 was just the beginning.Nearly 14 years later, Reid says 26 Shirts has created more than 1,000 Buffalo designs, helped more than 600 families and raised more than $2.3 million for families and charitable organizations."Sometimes it's like, all I did was blink and now we're here," Reid said.Reid is quick to share credit for the success of 26 Shirts by pointing to his team and Western New York's willingness to rally around people in need."I think it's the City of Good Neighbors," Reid said. "I don't think it's even specific to Bills fans. I think Bills fans live in Western New York. Western New York is a very giving community."WATCH: 26 Shirts enters 14th year of giving backFor Reid, the designs have become reminders of the people behind them."It's two thing

local.title: Delevan community rallies behind owners of Rusty Nail Tavern after weekend fire
local.summary: The Delevan community is rallying behind the owners of the Rusty Nail Tavern Restaurant after a fire damaged the popular dining destination over the weekend.
local.body: The Delevan community is rallying behind the owners of the Rusty Nail Tavern Restaurant after a fire damaged the popular dining destination over the weekend.On Friday, dozens of firefighters responded to the blaze on N Main Street. Fire departments from Delevan, Yorkshire, Machias, West Valley, Franklinville, Farmersville, Ischua, Ellicottville and more were on the scene.“We were sitting there for probably about an hour and one of the waitresses smelled some smoke," John Hoffman, a Delevan resident who was dining at the tavern, told WKBW on Monday. "About a half hour everybody was smelling more smoke, and then the manager Jen finally called 911."Hoffman and Crissi Lukowski, another Delevan resident, left prior to emergency crews' arrival, but were able to survey the damage the following day."It was really shocking," Lukowski told WKBW. "I used to work there before it was the Rusty Nail, and it was Hardee's Tavern for a long time. It was there for over 40 years."WATCH: Delevan community rallies behind owners of Rusty Nail Tavern after weekend fire"Delavan's doesn't have a lot of businesses anymore, so it was nice to see somebody investing in the community," Lukowski said.WKBW reached out to the owners of the Rusty Nail, but was told they were unavailable. However, one of the owners did address the community during a Facebook Live on Sunday. "We want to take a quick second, tell everybody a huge thank you for your love and support, and that everybody's been coming together, trying to get this place back up and running before we know it," the user told viewers. They added that plans are in the works to auction off surviving items from the tavern later this week.Other members of the community were quick to show their support in the wake of the fire.One user wrote, "We lost a bright spot in our little village last night as the Rusty Nail (formerly Hardy's Tavern) was lost in a fire." The post added, "We can only hope she chooses to rebuild and reopen in the same location and come together as a village to support her in that monumental effort"Assemblyman David DiPietro of Assembly District 147 wrote:Other neighboring businesses shared their support:The cause of the fire has not been released at this time. A GoFundMe has been established for the Rusty Nail Tavern Restaurant to help cover the costs of rebuilding.

JISOO has high praise for Han Chong, founder and creative director of self-portrait, noting that “I always feel like myself in the clothes no matter what I’m doing, and that is a very unique skill.” With this latest project, she continues, “I think we managed to show this in an entertaining way – the way that our world constantly moves around us, but that there is strength in being completely and effortlessly yourself. entertainment.title: ‘Aroma’ Takes a Sensory Trip Into Loneliness, Fantasy and Forbidden Desire (Exclusive Tallinn Trailer, Chat)
entertainment.summary: Xue Ma's third feature, a dark fairy tale that blurs the lines between "reality" and the subconscious, including dreams, premieres in Tallinn’s Rebels With a Cause competition.
entertainment.body:
Her sense of smell dominates Yang’s life. Due to a rare condition, most odors are unbearable for her – except for the smell of lemons and disinfectant. But one day, an unfamiliar scent leads her to a stranger, Fang. It turns out, though, that he is in a coma. Despite his state, Fang is trapped inside – in a life where childhood, fantasy and forbidden desire overlap and blend. His sister, who supported them as a masseuse, returns as a woman in red. And somewhere, the borders between the living, the lost, the dreamed and the imagined are starting to blur for Yang and Fang. Related Stories Movies Claes Bang, Valerie Pachner Drama 'I Is Another' Sells Wide Ahead of AFM Business The Hollywood Reporter Launches Turkish Edition

This is the story – well, part of it – of writer-director Xue Ma’s Aroma ( Hõng ), her third feature film after White River and Sonata of Wave . If you sense that her new film sounds, looks and feels offbeat, it is just fitting that it will world premiere in the Rebels With a Cause Competition section of the 30th edition of Estonia’s Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival ( PÖFF ) on Nov. 16.

In Aroma , Jiali Zhao stars as Yang, while Weihao Xu portrays Fang. Ze Ying and Lu Huang also feature in the cast. The cinematographer is Ash Chen, with editing by Maxime Pozzi-Garcia.

The filmmaker “turns smell into an invisible passage between reality and the subconscious,” the PÖFF website teases audiences about the dark fairy tale. “Ash Chen’s hypnotic cinematography gives texture to unstable memories, drawing us from clinical stillness into a dream-world glowing with danger and desire. Sensuous, unsettling and quietly provocative, Aroma keeps its deepest secret just beyond reach. Fang may be trapped inside his fantasy – but what if he is not the only one caught there?”

The filmmaker talked to THR about the themes she explored in the film. But before you read about what she shared below, THR can exclusively premiere the trailer for Aroma . Since the film is created as a stylized feast for the senses, we won’t keep you from watching, hearing and feeling the exclusive trailer. And we wonder if your sense of smell may also get stimulated…

“Cinema lets people experience feelings,” Ma tells THR about her approach to the many sensuous elements that Aroma provides. “I always imagine what cinematic language to use. I think it’s very interesting to experiment and share with others a common [sensory] experience – from the visual and sound to the smell and touch” and to connect that to emotions.
